passage: I'm Pankaj. When I moved to Bengaluru for my first job, my gaming squad became my whole evening. Six hours some nights. I told myself I couldn't be lonely with voices in my headset. Three months in, I noticed I hadn't spoken aloud to anyone since Monday. I didn't want to give up the squad; they were the ones who had asked how my interview went and celebrated when I got the job. Then Uma, who plays with us, mentioned she lived in Indiranagar too. We met for filter coffee and were awkward for ten minutes, then not. I still play most nights, but Saturday mornings I now walk with Uma and two of her friends. The squad knows, and they cheer me on. Looking back, I needed both kinds of company.

qa.q: Which city did Pankaj move to for a first job?
Why was Pankaj reluctant to give up the squad, and what does that show?
qa.a: The squad had asked how the interview went and celebrated the job, so Pankaj felt cared for and valued them.

qa.q: What is a balanced way for Pankaj to spend evenings and weekends?
qa.a: Pankaj can keep playing with the squad most nights and keep the Saturday walks with Uma and her friends, so online and in-person company sit side by side.

qa.q: How might Uma see meeting Pankaj for filter coffee?
qa.a: Uma may see it as a natural step from friendly voices to a real friend, since Uma mentioned living in Indiranagar too and later walks with Pankaj on Saturdays.

grounding: Pankaj relies on online friends yet values them while also building in-person connection.

passage: Honestly, in my first year in Bhopal, my closest friends were four people I'd never met. I'm Kalyani, by the way, and I'm not embarrassed about it. Every night at ten we'd log on to the same strategy game, and Simran, who lives in Nagpur, would say 'report, Captain' in a silly voice until I laughed. When I had a fever, it was the team that sent me soup through a food-delivery app. They were real to me. But one Saturday I realised I hadn't spoken out loud to anyone in my own city for three days. Not the security guard, not my classmates. That scared me a little. So I kept the ten o'clock games, and I also joined the college astronomy club on Fridays. Simran was the one who pushed me: 'Go look at real stars, Captain.' Now I have both. I still log on. I also know the guard's name.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel on realising three days had passed without speaking aloud?
qa.a: Kalyani felt a little scared, uneasy at how cut off life in the city had become.
Keeping the ten o'clock games while joining the astronomy club on Fridays, so online friends did not replace in-person ones.

qa.q: How does Simran seem to see Kalyani joining the club?
qa.a: Simran is supportive rather than jealous, even pushing Kalyani to 'go look at real stars'.

grounding: A spoken account values online friends while noticing they had replaced all in-person contact, and adding a real-world club.

passage:
Monday: Nitin had been in Guwahati five weeks and in his hostel room for most of them. His headset was his company: Nazia and the others from the online quiz league, voices he knew better than his roommate's. He skipped lunch in the mess again.
Thursday: During a late-night round, Nazia said, 'You've been online every time I log in. Do you ever go outside?' He laughed it off, but lay awake afterwards, thinking how the only face he'd seen that day was the mess cashier's.
The next Sunday: He left the headset on the desk and went down to the hostel's evening football. He was bad at it. A second-year called Rituraj passed to him anyway and asked where he was from. That night Nitin logged on for an hour, told Nazia about the match, and logged off before midnight.

qa.q: How long had Nitin been in Guwahati?
qa.a: Nitin had been in Guwahati five weeks.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling as he lay awake on Thursday?
qa.a: Nitin felt uneasy and lonely, realising the only face he had seen that day was the mess cashier's.

qa.q: What small step changed things for Nitin?
qa.a: Leaving the headset and going to the hostel football, while still keeping a shorter hour online with Nazia.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Nitin always being online?
qa.a: Nazia seems concerned and cares enough to ask whether he ever goes outside.

grounding: Shows online friends replacing all real contact, then Nitin keeping them while adding an in-person activity.
